Cocaine is a powerful, addictive stimulant drug derived from the coca plant. It affects the brain by increasing levels of dopamine and other chemicals, often producing short-lived feelings of euphoria, alertness, and energy.

It may be sold as a white powder or processed into “crack” cocaine, which is smoked. Use can cause serious risks, including rapid heart rate, high blood pressure, anxiety, dependence, heart attack, stroke, overdose, and death. Mixing cocaine with alcohol is especially dangerous because it can form a toxic compound called cocaethylene.

If someone may have overdosed—especially with chest pain, seizures, severe agitation, trouble breathing, or collapse—call emergency services immediately.

Cocaine is a powerful, highly addictive stimulant drug derived from the coca plant. It affects the brain by increasing levels of dopamine and other neurotransmitters, producing temporary feelings of energy, alertness, confidence, and euphoria.

It’s commonly found as a white powder, and “crack” is a smokable form. Cocaine can be snorted, injected, or smoked; all routes carry serious risks, including heart attack, stroke, seizures, overheating, psychosis, dependence, and overdose. Mixing it with alcohol is especially dangerous because the body can form a toxic chemical called cocaethylene.

Cocaine is illegal in many countries, though limited medical uses exist in some places. If someone may have overdosed—especially with chest pain, difficulty breathing, seizure, severe agitation, or loss of consciousness—call emergency services immediately.
